narrative.note: This first full look at Riley gives you a clear, honest starting line across every subject, and that clarity is exactly what makes the month ahead easy to plan.

subjects.math: Right now Riley is still building the skill of counting objects one at a time and saying how many there are. That's the next step to watch for.
subjects.literacy: Noticing what written words say, like a sign or a cereal box, hasn't clicked for Riley just yet. That curiosity about print is the next step here.
subjects.phonics: Clapping out the beats in a word, like ba-na-na, is still new ground for Riley. That's the next step for phonics.
subjects.writing: Riley is still developing the fingertip grip that lets a crayon move with control instead of a fist. That grip is the next step to build toward.
subjects.language: Telling you about something that happened earlier in the day is still forming for Riley. That storytelling piece is the next step for language.
subjects.science: Sorting things into groups, like big versus small or animals versus plants, is still coming together for Riley. That sorting sense is the next step for science.
subjects.social_studies: Naming family members and how they connect, like grandma being mommy's mom, is still new for Riley. That family map is the next step for social studies.
subjects.art: Naming colors while drawing or painting hasn't shown up yet for Riley. That color language is the next step for art.
subjects.music: Clapping or tapping along to a steady beat is still forming for Riley. That sense of rhythm is the next step for music.
subjects.gross_motor: Galloping, with one foot leading the other, is still new ground for Riley. That coordinated stride is the next step for gross motor.
subjects.fine_motor: Stringing large beads or threading laces is still developing for Riley. That pinching motion is the next step for fine motor.
subjects.social_emotional: Playing WITH other kids, taking turns and sharing with reminders, is still forming for Riley. That shared play is the next step for social-emotional growth.
subjects.self_care: Using the toilet during the day, with only occasional misses, is still coming together for Riley. That daytime independence is the next step for self-care.
subjects.executive_function: Waiting a short turn without falling apart, even with support, is still new for Riley. That patience is the next step for executive function.
subjects.computer_science: Giving exact step-by-step instructions during play, and following yours, hasn't come up yet for Riley. This one moves at your family's own pace, whenever you like.
subjects.spanish: Understanding common everyday words like water, milk, or more is still new ground for Riley in a second language. This one grows only as much as your family invites it in.

drawers.math: One-to-one counting, touching each object while saying the number, is a big leap for little counters. The stair-counting game turns that practice into something to look forward to each day.
drawers.literacy: Noticing that print carries meaning is the spark that makes reading matter to a child. A daily letter hunt turns everyday things like cereal boxes and street signs into a game worth playing.
drawers.phonics: Hearing a word break into parts is the foundation sound-based reading rests on. Sound I-spy is an easy way to build that ear anywhere, the car, the bath, or the grocery line.
drawers.writing: A fingertip grip usually shows up through drawing and play before it shows up on paper. Writing Riley's name big in marker, then tracing it in two more colors, gives that grip a fun reason to form.
drawers.language: Retelling a recent event in order is a skill that grows through practice, not instruction. Handing Riley the story after something fun happens, like asking them to describe the park, gives practice narrating it themselves.
drawers.science: Sorting is how early scientists organize the world before they can explain it. The sink or float game turns guessing into the whole point, no explanation needed yet.
drawers.social_studies: Understanding family roles is how young kids start to place themselves inside a bigger story. Drawing a map of your home together, with a star for everyone's bed, makes that story concrete and fun to build.
drawers.art: Naming colors while creating links language directly to what Riley's hands are doing. Playing one song and drawing how it feels, fast scribbles for fast parts, is a low-pressure way to get those color words flowing.
drawers.music: Keeping a beat is an early rhythm skill that shows up before most formal music learning. Copy my clap, where you clap a pattern and Riley echoes it, builds that ear with nothing more than hands.
drawers.gross_motor: Galloping asks for balance and coordination that build on top of running and jumping. Animal races down the hallway, a new animal each round, work that coordination while it just feels like play.
drawers.fine_motor: That pinching and threading motion is what later supports buttons, zippers, and handwriting. Snipping paper strips into confetti is a five-minute way to build the same small hand muscles.
drawers.social_emotional: Turn-taking with peers is a skill most four-year-olds are still learning with support, not one they arrive with already. Naming the feeling first, then offering two choices for what happens next, gives Riley a script to use in the moment.
drawers.self_care: This skill often clicks all at once once a child is ready, and there's nothing to rush ahead of that. The button board turns practice buttoning into a race against a timer instead of a morning struggle.
drawers.executive_function: Waiting is one of the hardest skills for a four-year-old brain to hold onto, so support here is expected, not a workaround. Freeze dance turns that waiting practice into a game: music stops, body stops.
drawers.computer_science: This one is about what your family chooses to do together, not a milestone with a clock on it. Robot parent, where Riley programs you across the room with exact steps, wrong steps included, makes debugging start as giggles.
drawers.spanish: Like coding, this grows only as much as your family invites it in, with no set pace to match. Picking one useful phrase and using it all week at natural moments is a small, doable way to start.
